Reproducing Mountoufaris et al. (2024) from dandiset 001131: rSLDS fits, seeds 0 and 1¶

Paper. Mountoufaris G, Nair A, et al. (2024), Cell 187, 5998-6015, doi:10.1016/j.cell.2024.08.015; the claims file was written from the accepted author manuscript (PMC11490375). Dandiset DANDI:001131, version 0.260601.1203, the most recent published version (it holds the two files of the earlier version, 0.240826.1647, and eight more; see reproduce_mountoufaris_2024.ipynb, which also holds the data checks).

The claims file asks for fits with seeds 0 to 3, each claim's outcome being the one all seeds give. One fit of all ten mice takes about 15 min on four cores, so the seeds are split over two notebooks, each under the 60-min limit: this one fits seeds 0 and 1. The outcome of each claim combines both notebooks and is given in the attempt record; the conclusions here are for these seeds.

Settings (claims file, fig6-rslds-fit-quality, from the ssm notebook the paper's code points to): one model per mouse, 3 discrete states, 5 latent dimensions, recurrent_only transitions, diagonal_gaussian dynamics, gaussian_orthog emissions, single subspace, Laplace-EM with a structured mean-field posterior, 100 iterations, 0.1 s bins, and alpha=0.0 in the fit call, as in that notebook (a full parameter update at each iteration; the first run of this attempt used ssm's default, 0.5). All ten mice have at least 31 units. The files hold only the male-intruder part of each session, so the two readings of which frames are fit (the male-intruder part, or the whole session) are the same: the whole file. The files hold z-scored traces; the sigma-normalized reading is fit for seed 0 in rslds_checks.ipynb, which also gives a held-out score.

t0 = time.time()
fits = vmh.fit_all(mice, seeds=SEEDS)
print(f"{len(fits)} fits in {(time.time() - t0) / 60:.1f} min")
S = {key: vmh.summarize_fit(f, M[key[0]]) for key, f in fits.items()}
rows = []
for (mouse, seed), s in sorted(S.items(), key=lambda kv: (G[kv[0][0]], kv[0])):
    f = fits[(mouse, seed)]
    rows.append({"mouse": mouse, "group": G[mouse], "seed": seed,
                 "elbo_first": f["elbos"][0], "elbo_last": f["elbos"][-1],
                 "elbo_change_last10_pct": 100 * (f["elbos"][-1] - f["elbos"][-11]) / abs(f["elbos"][-1]),
                 "r2": s["r2"], "fwd_r2_1s": vmh.forward_sim_score(f, 1.0), "fwd_r2_5s": vmh.forward_sim_score(f, 5.0),
                 "state_from": s["state_from"], "state": s["attack_state"],
                 "attack_in_state": s["attack_frac_in_state"],
                 **{f"occ{k}": s["state_occupancy"][k] for k in range(vmh.K_STATES)},
                 **{f"tau{j + 1}_a": s["tau_a"][j] for j in range(vmh.D_LATENT)},
                 **{f"tau{j + 1}_b": s["tau_b"][j] for j in range(vmh.D_LATENT)},
                 "score_a": s["score_a"], "score_b": s["score_b"]})
fit_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(fit_table.round(3).to_string(index=False))

tau*_a are the time constants (s) of the state holding most attack frames (reading (a); in mice 510 and 500, which have no attack annotation, the state holding most sniffing frames, state_from); tau*_b the mean over the three states (reading (b)). The ELBO's change over the last 10 iterations shows how far each fit had converged. A pair of complex eigenvalues gives two equal time constants, and so a line attractor score of 0 under the Methods' formula.

Link to the authors' fits¶

Mice 510 and 500 carry the authors' weights of each unit on "latent factor 1". If these fits find the same integration dimension, the weights of their first dimension should correlate with them.

rows = []
for (mouse, seed), s in S.items():
    w = M[mouse]["rslds_weights"]
    if w is None:
        continue
    r = {"mouse": mouse, "seed": seed}
    for j in range(vmh.D_LATENT):
        r[f"dim{j + 1}"] = abs(stats.spearmanr(np.abs(w), s["weights"][:, j])[0])
    rows.append(r)

Claim fig6-rslds-fit-quality¶

rSLDS models with 5 latent dimensions and 3 discrete states, fit to each mouse with at least 31 units, capture about 85% of the variance, with similar performance in control and experimental mice; attack occurs within a single rSLDS state in both groups.

Variance explained is the R2 of the emissions reconstruction (claims file). Performance is the R2 of forward predictions of the latents over 1 s and 5 s; the paper computes it on held-out folds, which would take five more fits per mouse and seed and is not run here, so it is computed on the fit data.

In [5]:
rows = []
for seed in SEEDS:
    d = fit_table[fit_table.seed == seed]
    c, e = d[d.group == "control"], d[d.group == "experimental"]
    att = d[d.state_from == "attack"]
    rows.append({"seed": seed, "r2_control": c.r2.mean(), "r2_exp": e.r2.mean(),
                 "r2_min": d.r2.min(), "r2_max": d.r2.max(),
                 "fwd1_control": c.fwd_r2_1s.mean(), "fwd1_exp": e.fwd_r2_1s.mean(),
                 "p_fwd1": vmh.mw(c.fwd_r2_1s, e.fwd_r2_1s)[1],
                 "fwd5_control": c.fwd_r2_5s.mean(), "fwd5_exp": e.fwd_r2_5s.mean(),
                 "p_fwd5": vmh.mw(c.fwd_r2_5s, e.fwd_r2_5s)[1],

                 "attack_90pct_one_state": int((att.attack_in_state >= 0.9).sum()),
                 "attack_in_state_min": att.attack_in_state.min()})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3).to_string(index=False))

Result: not reproduced for seeds 0 and 1. The fits explain 59% of the variance in both groups (0.594 control, 0.585 and 0.587 experimental; range 0.495 to 0.663 over mice), against 85 +/- 8.5%. The forward-prediction R2 does not differ between groups (Mann-Whitney p = 0.114 at 1 s and 5 s, both seeds), though it is computed on the fit data; rslds_checks.ipynb gives a held-out score. Attack frames fall mostly in one state in 7 (seed 0) and 8 (seed 1) of the 8 mice with attack annotations, and at least 90% in one state in 3 and 2 of them. The first fit dimension of mice 510 and 500 does not match the authors' latent factor 1 (|Spearman r| at most 0.47); the best match of any dimension is 0.70 (mouse 500, seed 1, dimension 4).

Claim fig6a-control-tau1-greater¶

In control mice, the time constant of the first rSLDS dimension (about 100-120 s) is significantly larger than that of the second (about 40 s).

In [6]:
def tau_tests(group):
    rows = []
    for seed in SEEDS:
        d = fit_table[(fit_table.seed == seed) & (fit_table.group == group)]
        for reading in ("a", "b"):
            T = d[[f"tau{j + 1}_{reading}" for j in range(vmh.D_LATENT)]].to_numpy()
            kw = stats.kruskal(*T.T)
            rows.append({"seed": seed, "reading": reading, "mice": len(T),
                         **{f"mean_tau{j + 1}": T[:, j].mean() for j in range(vmh.D_LATENT)},
                         "kw_H": kw.statistic, "kw_p": kw.pvalue, "dunn_1v2_p": vmh.dunn_1_vs_2(T),
                         "tau1_largest_mean": bool(T[:, 0].mean() == T.mean(0).max())})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

ctl_tau = tau_tests("control")
print(ctl_tau.round(3).to_string(index=False))
print("expected control tau1 90 to 132 s, tau2 36 to 44 s")

 seed reading  mice  mean_tau1  mean_tau2  mean_tau3  mean_tau4  mean_tau5   kw_H  kw_p  dunn_1v2_p  tau1_largest_mean
    0       a     4    408.538    376.956    142.456     96.158     81.722  8.283 0.082         1.0               True
    0       b     4    414.297    294.318    144.081    102.407     77.015 13.528 0.009         1.0               True
    1       a     4    429.229    351.379    111.382     98.626     84.126 12.512 0.014         1.0               True
    1       b     4    963.924    705.852    149.741    118.808     82.872 15.574 0.004         1.0               True
expected control tau1 90 to 132 s, tau2 36 to 44 s

Result: not reproduced for seeds 0 and 1. Control time constants are far longer than the paper's: mean tau1 409 to 964 s and tau2 294 to 706 s over seeds and readings, against 90 to 132 s and 36 to 44 s. Kruskal-Wallis across the five sorted dimensions gives p from 0.004 to 0.082 (above 0.05 for seed 0, reading (a)), and Dunn's comparison of dimension 1 with 2 gives p = 1.0 in every case.

Claim fig6c-experimental-tau-indistinguishable¶

In experimental mice the first two rSLDS dimensions have statistically indistinguishable time constants (below 50 s), because the first dimension's time constant is reduced relative to controls.

Result: not reproduced for seeds 0 and 1. Experimental mean tau1 is 269 to 546 s and tau2 141 to 424 s, not below 55 s. The paper's Kruskal-Wallis test over the five dimensions finds a difference (p from below 0.001 to 0.002), while Dunn's comparison of dimension 1 with 2 does not (p = 1.0). Control tau1 is not longer than experimental tau1 at p < 0.01 under any seed or reading (two-sided p = 0.17, 0.76, 0.35 and 0.038), and in two of the four cases the experimental mean is the longer.

Claim fig6f-line-attractor-score¶

The line attractor score, log2 of the ratio of the two largest time constants, is about 1.6 in control mice and close to zero in experimental mice.

Result: not reproduced for seeds 0 and 1. The mean control score is 0.22 to 1.05 (expected 1.44 to 1.76) and the experimental mean 0.36 to 0.78; the Mann-Whitney test finds no difference (p from 0.58 to 1.0). Many scores are 0 because the two slowest eigenvalues are a complex pair.

Claim fig6g-flow-field-line-vs-point¶

Flow fields of the fit rSLDS in the plane of the first two principal components show a line attractor (a roughly linear region of low flow) in control mice and a point attractor in experimental mice.

Judged per mouse by the line attractor score (claims file). The flow field of the state used for reading (a) is drawn for every mouse, for the first seed of this notebook (mice 510 and 500 are the ones whose files the authors chose as exemplars).

In [9]:
rows = []
for seed in SEEDS:
    d = fit_table[fit_table.seed == seed]
    for reading in ("a", "b"):
        c, e = d[d.group == "control"][f"score_{reading}"], d[d.group == "experimental"][f"score_{reading}"]
        rows.append({"seed": seed, "reading": reading, "control_above_1": f"{int((c > 1).sum())} of {len(c)}",
                     "exp_below_1": f"{int((e < 1).sum())} of {len(e)}",

order = sorted(M, key=lambda k: (G[k], k))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(20, 8))
for ax, mouse in zip(axes.ravel(), order):
    f, s = fits[(mouse, SEEDS[0])], S[(mouse, SEEDS[0])]
    x = f["x"]
    mu = x.mean(0)
    _, _, Vt = np.linalg.svd(x - mu, full_matrices=False)
    P = Vt[:2].T                       # latent -> first two PCs
    pc = (x - mu) @ P
    g1, g2 = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(*np.percentile(pc[:, 0], [1, 99]), 25),
                         np.linspace(*np.percentile(pc[:, 1], [1, 99]), 25))
    grid = mu + np.column_stack([g1.ravel(), g2.ravel()]) @ P.T
    A, b = f["As"][s["attack_state"]], f["bs"][s["attack_state"]]
    dx = (grid @ A.T + b - grid) @ P
    speed = np.linalg.norm(dx, axis=1)
    ax.contourf(g1, g2, np.log10(speed.reshape(g1.shape)), 20, cmap="Greys_r")
    ax.quiver(g1, g2, dx[:, 0].reshape(g1.shape), dx[:, 1].reshape(g1.shape), color="tab:blue")
    ax.plot(pc[:, 0], pc[:, 1], "r", lw=0.3, alpha=0.5)
    ax.set(title=f"{mouse} ({G[mouse][:3]}), seed {SEEDS[0]}, state {s['attack_state']}, score {s['score_a']:.2f}",
           xlabel="PC1", ylabel="PC2")
    inside = np.mean((pc[:, 0] >= g1.min()) & (pc[:, 0] <= g1.max()) & (pc[:, 1] >= g2.min()) & (pc[:, 1] <= g2.max()))
    slow = np.column_stack([g1.ravel(), g2.ravel()])[np.argsort(speed)[:25]]   # the 4% slowest grid points
    spread = np.linalg.svd(slow - slow.mean(0), compute_uv=False)
    print(f"{mouse}: slowest-flow points elongation (SD ratio of their two axes) {spread[0] / max(spread[1], 1e-12):.1f}; speed range {speed.min():.4f} to {speed.max():.4f} per bin; "
          f"{100 * (1 - inside):.1f}% of trajectory points outside the axes; score_a {s['score_a']:.2f}")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Result: not reproduced for seeds 0 and 1. At most 2 of the 4 control mice have a score above 1 under any seed and reading (0, 1, 1 and 2 of 4), so a majority never does; 5 or 6 of the 6 experimental mice have a score below 1. The flow fields of all ten mice are drawn above for seed 0. Their slowest-flow grid points form an elongated region (ratio of the two axes above 4) in 1 of the 4 control mice (482, ratio 18.8) and in 3 of the 6 experimental mice (440, 497, 501; ratios 4.5, 7.6 and 13.0), and a compact one in the others (ratios 1.2 to 2.7), so the shapes do not split by group as the paper's line and point attractors do.

Claim fig7b-achw-first-dimension¶

The mean autocorrelation half-width of units weighted on the first rSLDS dimension, over the entire male-male interaction, is shorter in experimental (9.86 +/- 1 s) than in control mice (28.6 +/- 1.23 s); the reduction is about 66%, against about 61% for second-dimension units.

ACHW per unit over the whole interaction (first annotated behaviour to the end of the file). ACHW is the same for z-scored and sigma-normalized traces (an affine map does not change the autocorrelation), and with one intruder per file the "mean over trials" reading is the single autocorrelation, so the readings left are which units are "weighted on" a dimension: (a) the dimension of each unit's largest weight, (b) the top 25% of units by weight on that dimension. The estimator of the autocorrelation is open (see vmh.achw): the window-mean, biased estimator decides here, and the two others are shown. When the two slowest eigenvalues are a complex pair, dimension 2 takes the weights of the imaginary part of the pair's eigenvector (vmh.summarize_fit).

In [10]:

Result: not reproduced for seeds 0 and 1. The ACHW of first-dimension units is shorter in experimental mice under every combination (window-mean biased estimator: pooled means 19.5 to 23.1 s against 29.6 to 33.6 s; over all three estimators 19.5 to 30.3 s against 29.6 to 43.8 s; pooled Mann-Whitney p < 0.001; on per-mouse means p = 0.11 to 0.76). The experimental values are two to three times the paper's 9.86 +/- 1 s in every combination; one control value falls inside 28.6 +/- 1.23 s (29.6 s, seed 1, largest weight, biased estimator). The second-dimension reduction is 22 to 60% pooled and 4 to 73% on per-mouse means, inside 61 +/- 6.1% in a few combinations (57.8 to 60.4% pooled, seed 0, largest weight). With the imaginary part of a complex pair now giving dimension 2 its own weights (complex pairs in 4 mice for seed 0 and 8 for seed 1), every combination is defined.

Blocked claim fig6e-integration-dimension-persistence, a variant¶

The files do not mark when the intruder is removed, so the post-intruder period of Figure 6E cannot be found. As a variant that does not decide the outcome, the first dimension's activity (projection of the latents on the first eigenvector of the reading (a) state, normalized to 0-1 per mouse) is compared between all frames of annotated behaviour and the frames after the last annotated behaviour.

In [11]:
rows = []
for (mouse, seed), s in S.items():
    m, f = M[mouse], fits[(mouse, seed)]
    A = f["As"][s["attack_state"]]
    tau, V = vmh.time_constants(A)
    p = f["x"] @ np.real(V[:, 0])
    p = (p - p.min()) / (p.max() - p.min())
    n = len(p)
    beh = np.zeros(n, bool)
    for b in m["bouts"].values():
        beh |= vmh.frames(b, n)
    last = int(max(b[-1, 1] for b in m["bouts"].values()) * m["rate"])
    first = int(vmh.first_behaviour_s(m) * m["rate"])
    if first > 0 and p[beh].mean() < p[:first].mean():
        p = 1 - p                      # orient the axis so that activity during bouts is above the pre-interaction level
    on_bouts, after = p[beh].mean(), p[last:].mean()
    rows.append({"mouse": mouse, "group": m["group"], "seed": seed, "after_s": (n - last) / m["rate"],
                 "during_bouts": on_bouts, "after_last_bout": after})
post = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(post.round(3).to_string(index=False))
for seed in SEEDS:
    for g in ("control", "experimental"):
        d = post[(post.seed == seed) & (post.group == g)]
        t = stats.ttest_rel(d.during_bouts, d.after_last_bout)
        print(f"seed {seed} {g}: during {d.during_bouts.mean():.3f}, after {d.after_last_bout.mean():.3f}, "
              f"paired t = {t.statistic:.2f}, p = {t.pvalue:.3f}")

The sign of an eigenvector is arbitrary, so each mouse's axis is oriented so that activity during bouts is above the level before the first annotated behaviour; the variant shows whether activity on the slowest dimension differs after the last annotated behaviour, not whether it stays elevated after an intruder's removal.

In this variant no control comparison reaches p < 0.05 (seed 0 p = 0.47, seed 1 p = 0.43), and the experimental one does for seed 1 only (p = 0.049; seed 0 p = 0.77).

Summary¶

Claim Seeds 0 and 1
fig6-rslds-fit-quality not reproduced: variance explained 59%, not 85%
fig6a-control-tau1-greater not reproduced: control tau1 409 to 964 s; tau1 and tau2 not separated (Dunn p = 1.0)
fig6c-experimental-tau-indistinguishable not reproduced: experimental tau1 and tau2 well above 55 s; tau1 not lower than control at p < 0.01
fig6f-line-attractor-score not reproduced: control score 0.22 to 1.05
fig6g-flow-field-line-vs-point not reproduced: at most 2 of 4 control mice above 1
fig7b-achw-first-dimension not reproduced: experimental ACHW 19 to 30 s, not 9.9 s
fig6e-integration-dimension-persistence blocked, metadata insufficient
figs6f-mating-attractor-intact blocked, data missing

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's: the fits use the z-scored traces of the whole file (the files appear to hold only the male-intruder part), the performance score is computed on the fit data (a one-fold held-out score is in rslds_checks.ipynb), the estimator of the autocorrelation is not given (three are shown), and mice 510 and 500 have no attack annotation, so their reading (a) state is the one holding most sniffing frames. The fits do not recover the authors' latent factor 1 deposited for mice 510 and 500, so the fits here and the paper's may differ in ways the Methods do not let one find.
